title: Making an independent judgement about economic evidence
framing: In this formative assessment, you will examine an unfamiliar economic relationship and independently evaluate a causal claim. You will bring together your understanding of statistical evidence and economic reasoning to produce one integrated judgement. After completing your evaluation, you will have an opportunity to compare your reasoning with explanatory feedback and an example evaluation.
attempt_instructions:
Allow approximately 15 minutes for this assessment.

Spend the first 11 minutes examining the supplied evidence and writing your independent evaluation. Everything you need for the task is provided. You do not need to consult earlier activities, undertake external research or perform additional statistical calculations.

Write one coherent evaluation rather than a series of separate answers. Approximately 100–150 words is a useful guide, but the quality of your reasoning matters more than its length.

Use the remaining four minutes to review the feedback, compare it with your evaluation and reconsider your reasoning. You do not need to write a second evaluation.

This assessment is formative. Its purpose is to help you understand how well you can bring your economic reasoning together independently. It does not contribute to a grade.

editorial_opening_image.subject: A contemporary administrative workplace
editorial_opening_image.context: A restrained editorial photograph establishing the professional setting of an economic evaluation concerning vocational training and employee productivity.
editorial_opening_image.caption_intent: Provide a neutral visual introduction to the workplace context without suggesting a relationship between training and productivity or contributing evidence to the assessment.
editorial_opening_image.detailed_description: A wide, landscape-format editorial photograph of a contemporary administrative office, viewed from a natural eye-level perspective. Show a small number of ordinary workstations with computer monitors, keyboards and unobtrusive office furnishings. Use soft natural daylight, balanced composition and a restrained, neutral colour palette. The office should feel credible and understated rather than promotional. Screens should contain no legible information. Do not depict a training session, managerial decisions, employee performance comparisons, productivity measurements, graphs, charts, causal relationships or contrasting employee behaviours. Do not imply that any individual is more experienced, motivated or productive than another. Include no embedded typography, labels, titles, slogans, numerical information, caption panels or explanatory graphics. The image is entirely decorative and must not be presented as a depiction of the eight employees in the synthetic dataset.

purpose.visibility_claim: Make visible the learner's independent capability to integrate statistical interpretation, causal reasoning and evidential judgement in an unfamiliar economic context. The initial constructed performance should provide interpretable evidence of whether the learner can accurately characterise an observed relationship, recognise what a causal claim asserts beyond the observations, generate and explain a plausible competing economic mechanism, evaluate the adequacy of the available evidence, justify a proposal for additional evidence and communicate a coherent, appropriately qualified conclusion. The evidence concerns the learner's demonstrated capability in this particular context, rather than establishing general mastery or certifying readiness for progression.
purpose.stop_rationale: This formative stop realises Learning Element 8, Making an independent judgement about economic evidence, within developmental phase 5, From supported reasoning to independent judgement. Following earlier experiences that progressively developed statistical interpretation, recognition of causal claims, explanation of competing mechanisms and judgement about additional evidence, learners now need an opportunity to integrate these capabilities without answer-bearing support. The reserved vocational training and employee productivity case, D09 from ECON-CORR-01, provides an unfamiliar context in which to examine independent transfer. A single coherent constructed performance preserves the intellectual demand of deciding how the relevant concepts work together. Separating the initial performance from explanatory feedback makes the learner's independent reasoning distinguishable from reasoning developed through subsequent support.
purpose.forward_intent: Enable learners to recognise the strengths, omissions and limitations of their independent evaluation and reconsider their reasoning in light of explanatory feedback. Feedback should support more accurate statistical interpretation, better-developed competing explanations, stronger justification of evidential limitations and additional evidence, and conclusions proportionate to the observations. The experience consolidates a conceptual foundation for subsequent formal study of econometrics without introducing formal econometric methods, determining progression or prescribing a subsequent learning pathway.

count_basis.rationale: The commission explicitly requires one coherent independent evaluation, identified as E1. No additional determinate components are necessary. Separate questions testing statistical interpretation, causal direction, confounding or methodological choices would fragment the commissioned performance and could supply conceptual cues that compromise the independence of the evidence. The six achievement dimensions are complementary perspectives on the same performance, not six separate assessment components.

evidence_rationale.approach: Elicit one integrated, non-determinate constructed performance using the reserved D09 case. Interpret the initial response across six connected achievement dimensions to establish a useful qualitative evidence profile at standard assessment depth. The breadth of evidence comes from the integration of different forms of reasoning within one authentic performance rather than from a larger number of assessment interactions.

achievement_dimensions.evidence_sought: Accurate contextual interpretation of the direction, strength and relevant characteristics of the observed relationship, consistent with the supplied scatterplot and Pearson correlation coefficient.
Recognition that the illustrative causal claim asserts an effect of providing additional vocational training on employee productivity, extending beyond a description of the observed association.

Independent generation and sufficient explanation of at least one economically plausible competing mechanism that could account for the observed relationship. The explanation should establish how the proposed mechanism could produce the association rather than merely naming a causal concept.
Reasoned evaluation of whether the supplied observations establish the causal claim, identifying relevant limitations and distinguishing plausible explanations from established findings.
Identification of relevant additional evidence or a more informative comparison, accompanied by an explanation of how it would address an unresolved causal issue and strengthen causal interpretation.
A coherent, integrated evaluation culminating in an appropriately qualified conclusion that is consistent with the statistical evidence, competing explanations and acknowledged uncertainty.

interpretive_principles: Interpret the six achievement dimensions as connected aspects of a single economic judgement.
Distinguish evidence of accurate statistical interpretation from evidence of adequate causal reasoning.
Recognise economically defensible alternative mechanisms and proposals for additional evidence without requiring predetermined wording or an exhaustive inventory of causal concepts.
Distinguish an unexplained assertion from a sufficiently developed mechanism or justification.
Treat omissions as capabilities not demonstrated in this performance, rather than definitive evidence that the learner lacks those capabilities.
Recognise that a justified conclusion requires more than repeating the general principle that correlation does not establish causation.
Prioritise explanatory adequacy, coherence and evidential proportionality over response length.
Do not assign numerical weights, grades, pass thresholds or progression decisions.
Do not introduce automatic correctness judgements, runtime AI marking or exact-answer matching for the constructed response.

response_scope.rationale: A concise extended response is sufficient to make the connected reasoning visible within the allocated time. Explanatory adequacy rather than compliance with a word limit determines the usefulness of the evidence.

elicitations.evidence_ask: Independently construct a coherent evaluation of the illustrative causal claim concerning vocational training and employee productivity. Integrate contextualised statistical interpretation, recognition of the causal assertion, explanation of at least one plausible competing economic mechanism, judgement about the adequacy of the supplied evidence, justification of relevant additional evidence and communication of an appropriately qualified conclusion. The performance should make the six connected achievement dimensions visible without decomposing them into separately prompted answers.
elicitations.stimulus:
Vocational training and employee productivity

The following synthetic data have been constructed for learning purposes. They do not report findings from an actual empirical study.

Eight illustrative employees perform broadly comparable administrative work during the same month. For each employee, two measurements are recorded: hours of vocational training completed during the month and administrative cases completed per working day. Both variables are measured during the same month. Training was not randomly allocated.

The scatterplot and accompanying data table present the eight employee observations. The Pearson correlation coefficient is r = 0.92.

Illustrative causal claim: Providing employees with additional vocational training increases their productivity.

Bring your reasoning together in a justified conclusion.

materials.body:
Reviewing your independent evaluation

Compare your evaluation with the following explanation of what makes an economic judgement well supported. These are connected qualities of your overall evaluation, not six separately marked answers.

Statistical interpretation

The scatterplot and Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.92 indicate a strong positive, approximately linear relationship. Employees who completed more vocational training generally completed more administrative cases per working day in this illustrative sample. The relationship is not exact: employees with more training did not invariably complete more cases. The coefficient describes the strength and direction of the linear association; it does not measure the productivity gain caused by training.

Claim recognition

The claim goes beyond describing differences between employees. It asserts that providing additional training would increase productivity compared with what would otherwise happen. Observing that employees with more training tend to be more productive does not establish what would happen if an employee received additional training.

Alternative explanation

Training could improve relevant knowledge and skills, enabling employees to complete more cases. However, more productive employees might also be selected for additional training because managers expect greater returns from investing in them. This would provide a possible reverse causal explanation. Alternatively, motivation could influence both participation in training and the number of cases completed, providing a possible common causal influence. These mechanisms could coexist. A well-developed alternative explanation shows how the proposed mechanism could produce the observed relationship, rather than simply naming reverse causality or a confounding variable. Other economically plausible mechanisms are equally appropriate when their reasoning is sufficiently explained.

Evidential judgement

Training and productivity were measured during the same month, so the observations do not establish which relevant changes occurred first. Training was not randomly allocated, and the dataset does not provide information about previous productivity, prior experience, motivation, managerial decisions or differences in case complexity. Consequently, the observed differences between employees cannot confidently be attributed to training alone. The strong association is compatible with a beneficial effect of training, but it does not establish that effect. Equally, the evidence does not establish that training has no effect.

Further evidence

Useful additional evidence should address a specific uncertainty. Previous productivity records could help investigate whether employees who undertook more training were already more productive. Information about how training opportunities were allocated could help assess whether selection influenced the observed relationship. A suitably designed study that randomly allocated additional training opportunities and compared subsequent productivity could reduce systematic pre-existing differences between groups and provide a more informative causal comparison. Such a study would still require appropriate implementation and measurement. Other proposals are defensible if you explain how they would help distinguish competing explanations. Collecting more observations of the same two variables might improve the descriptive evidence but would not, by itself, resolve the causal uncertainty.

Communication

A convincing conclusion connects the statistical evidence, plausible explanations and limitations of the observations. It acknowledges the strength of the observed relationship without treating that strength as proof of causation. It also explains why the proposed additional evidence would make a causal interpretation more credible. Your wording need not match the examples above; what matters is whether your reasoning supports your conclusion.

An example of an integrated evaluation

The scatterplot and correlation coefficient of 0.92 show a strong positive, approximately linear association: employees completing more training generally complete more cases per day. However, the claim asserts that providing additional training would itself increase productivity. Training could improve relevant skills, but more productive employees might be selected for further training. Motivation could also influence both training participation and productivity. Because both variables were measured during the same month and training was not randomly allocated, the observations cannot distinguish these explanations. Previous productivity records could help establish whether employees undertaking more training were already more productive. Randomly allocating additional training opportunities and comparing subsequent productivity could reduce systematic pre-existing differences between groups. The evidence is therefore consistent with a beneficial effect of training, but does not establish that effect.

This is one defensible evaluation, not the only acceptable response. Your evaluation may develop different plausible mechanisms or propose different additional evidence while reaching a similarly well-justified judgement.

formative_return.forward_orientation: Return to your initial evaluation and identify the aspect of your reasoning that would benefit most from improvement. Consider whether your interpretation was accurate, whether your competing explanation showed how the observed relationship could arise, and whether your proposed additional evidence addressed a specific uncertainty. Reconsider your conclusion in light of these connections. You do not need to write another evaluation.

assessment_evidence.pack_forward_orientation: When you encounter another economic causal claim, apply the same integrated approach: interpret the observed evidence accurately, distinguish what is observed from what is being claimed, consider plausible competing explanations and identify evidence that would help distinguish them. Aim to make the strength of your conclusion proportionate to the strength of the evidence. These habits provide a foundation for later study of how economists investigate causal relationships more formally.
